references.authors: Cahill GF Jr
references.title: Fuel metabolism in starvation.
references.finding: Classic review of human starvation physiology: hepatic glycogen and gluconeogenesis carry the first day, then fat-derived ketones progressively replace glucose as brain fuel, sparing protein.

references.authors: Owen OE, Morgan AP, Kemp HG, et al.
references.title: Brain metabolism during fasting.
references.finding: Cerebral catheterisation after 5-6 weeks of starvation showed beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate had replaced glucose as the brain's predominant fuel.

references.authors: Owen OE, Felig P, Morgan AP, et al.
references.title: Liver and kidney metabolism during prolonged starvation.
references.finding: During prolonged starvation glucose and insulin fell over the first 3 days, while free fatty acids, beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate did not plateau until after ~17 days.

references.authors: Rothman DL, Magnusson I, Katz LD, et al.
references.title: Quantitation of hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in fasting humans with 13C NMR.
references.finding: Serial liver 13C NMR over a 68-h fast: gluconeogenesis supplied 64% of glucose output in the first 22 h, 82% over the next 14 h and 96% over the following 18 h as liver glycogen ran down.

references.authors: Landau BR, Wahren J, Chandramouli V, et al.
references.title: Contributions of gluconeogenesis to glucose production in the fasted state.
references.finding: Gluconeogenesis contributed ~47% of glucose production after 14 h, 67% after 22 h and 93% after 42 h of fasting.

references.authors: Klein S, Sakurai Y, Romijn JA, et al.
references.title: Progressive alterations in lipid and glucose metabolism during short-term fasting in young adult men.
references.finding: Across 12-72 h of fasting, lipolysis doubled (60% of the rise by 24 h, largest step at 18-24 h), glucose fell ~25% (5.6 to 4.1 mmol/L) and insulin halved, with 70% of the insulin decline in the first 24 h.

references.authors: Ho KY, Veldhuis JD, Johnson ML, et al.
references.title: Fasting enhances growth hormone secretion and amplifies the complex rhythms of growth hormone secretion in man.
references.finding: By day 5 of a fast, 24-h integrated growth hormone rose ~3-fold (2.82 to 8.75 ug.min/mL) with more frequent, larger pulses.

references.authors: Hartman ML, Veldhuis JD, Johnson ML, et al.
references.title: Augmented growth hormone (GH) secretory burst frequency and amplitude mediate enhanced GH secretion during a two-day fast in normal men.
references.finding: Two days of fasting produced a ~5-fold increase in 24-h endogenous growth hormone production via more and larger secretory bursts.

references.authors: Clemmons DR, Klibanski A, Underwood LE, et al.
references.title: Reduction of plasma immunoreactive somatomedin C during fasting in humans.
references.finding: Ten days of fasting lowered plasma somatomedin C (IGF-1) from 0.83 to 0.21 U/mL, tracking nitrogen loss; it rose promptly with refeeding.

references.authors: Anton SD, Moehl K, Donahoo WT, et al.
references.title: Flipping the Metabolic Switch: Understanding and Applying the Health Benefits of Fasting.
references.finding: Defines the 'metabolic switch' from glucose to fatty acids/ketones as typically occurring 12-36 h after the last meal, depending on liver glycogen and activity.

references.authors: Steinhauser ML, Olenchock BA, O'Keefe J, et al.
references.title: The circulating metabolome of human starvation.
references.finding: Plasma metabolomics during a 10-day zero-calorie fast showed early consumption of gluconeogenic amino acids, then a surge of fatty acids marking the shift to lipid fuel, possibly driven by falling leptin.

references.authors: Teruya T, Chaleckis R, Takada J, et al.
references.title: Diverse metabolic reactions activated during 58-hr fasting are revealed by non-targeted metabolomic analysis of human blood.
references.finding: Non-targeted blood metabolomics during 34-58 h fasts found 44 metabolites up 1.5-60-fold, including pentose-phosphate and TCA-cycle compounds; authors propose antioxidant (NADPH) demand as a principal fasting response.

references.authors: Pietzner M, Uluvar B, Kolnes KJ, et al.
references.title: Systemic proteome adaptions to 7-day complete caloric restriction in humans.
references.finding: A 7-day water-only fast (mean -5.7 kg) produced >1,000 changing plasma proteins, but systemic proteome changes appeared only after ~3 days of fasting.

references.authors: Grundler F, Mesnage R, Ruppert PMM, et al.
references.title: Long-Term Fasting-Induced Ketosis in 1610 Subjects: Metabolic Regulation and Safety.
references.finding: In 4-21-day Buchinger fasts (~75-250 kcal/day) ketonuria was present in >95% from day 4; ketosis stayed far below ketoacidosis, and uric acid rose by ~100-200 umol/L, more with stronger ketosis.

references.authors: Halberg N, Henriksen M, Söderhamn N, et al.
references.title: Effect of intermittent fasting and refeeding on insulin action in healthy men.
references.finding: Beta-hydroxybutyrate was 0.06 mmol/L after an overnight fast and only 0.10 mmol/L after 20 h; 15 days of every-other-day 20-h fasts without weight loss improved insulin-mediated glucose uptake.

references.authors: Pan JW, Rothman TL, Behar KL, et al.
references.title: Human brain beta-hydroxybutyrate and lactate increase in fasting-induced ketosis.
references.finding: Brain beta-hydroxybutyrate rose from 0.05 to 0.60 mmol/L after 2 days and 0.98 mmol/L after 3 days of fasting; brain levels were about a quarter of plasma (slope 0.26).

references.authors: Buffet A, Vezzosi D, Maiza JC, et al.
references.title: Increased plasma β-hydroxybutyrate levels during the fasting test in patients with endogenous hyperinsulinaemic hypoglycaemia.
references.finding: People without insulinoma undergoing a supervised 72-h fast reached a median plasma beta-hydroxybutyrate of ~6.1 mmol/L at the end of the test, showing how high fasting ketosis can climb.

references.authors: Kerndt PR, Naughton JL, Driscoll CE, et al.
references.title: Fasting: the history, pathophysiology and complications.
references.finding: Weight loss averages ~0.9 kg/day in the first week of fasting (largely sodium and water) and ~0.3 kg/day by week 3; insulin and T3 fall, glucagon rises; complications include gout, urate stones, postural hypotension and arrhythmias.

references.authors: Alirezaei M, Kemball CC, Flynn CT, et al.
references.title: Short-term fasting induces profound neuronal autophagy.
references.finding: In mice, short-term (24-48 h) food restriction markedly increased autophagosomes in cortical neurons and Purkinje cells; the main source of the popular 'autophagy at 24-48 h' claim.

references.authors: Pietrocola F, Demont Y, Castoldi F, et al.
references.title: Metabolic effects of fasting on human and mouse blood in vivo.
references.finding: Fasting up to 4 days in humans changed the plasma metabolome and reduced leukocyte protein acetylation, but increased autophagic flux was detectable only in neutrophils and only with ex vivo protease inhibition.

references.authors: Vendelbo MH, Møller AB, Christensen B, et al.
references.title: Fasting increases human skeletal muscle net phenylalanine release and this is associated with decreased mTOR signaling.
references.finding: A 72-h fast halved muscle mTOR phosphorylation and raised LC3B-II ~30%, but p62 also rose ~10%, so autophagic flux could not be confirmed; net muscle protein release increased.

references.authors: Dethlefsen MM, Bertholdt L, Gudiksen A, et al.
references.title: Training state and skeletal muscle autophagy in response to 36 h of fasting.
references.finding: Muscle biopsies at 2-36 h of fasting showed only modest changes in autophagy markers (LC3, p62), in untrained men only; training status altered the response.

references.authors: Jamshed H, Beyl RA, Della Manna DL, et al.
references.title: Early Time-Restricted Feeding Improves 24-Hour Glucose Levels and Affects Markers of the Circadian Clock, Aging, and Autophagy in Humans.
references.finding: Four days of eating 8 am-2 pm vs 8 am-8 pm lowered 24-h glucose, raised morning beta-hydroxybutyrate to ~0.15 mmol/L, and increased whole-blood expression of SIRT1 and the autophagy gene LC3A.

references.authors: Bensalem J, Teong XT, Hattersley KJ, et al.
references.title: Intermittent time-restricted eating may increase autophagic flux in humans: an exploratory analysis.
references.finding: PBMC LC3B-II autophagic flux differed between intermittent fasting plus TRE and standard care at 6 months (post hoc, P = 0.04), partly because flux fell in controls; CR vs control was not significant.

references.authors: Bagherniya M, Butler AE, Barreto GE, et al.
references.title: The effect of fasting or calorie restriction on autophagy induction: A review of the literature.
references.finding: Review concluding fasting and CR are potent autophagy inducers, with the evidence coming overwhelmingly from cell and animal studies; human data are sparse.

references.authors: Shimazu T, Hirschey MD, Newman J, et al.
references.title: Suppression of oxidative stress by β-hydroxybutyrate, an endogenous histone deacetylase inhibitor.
references.finding: Beta-hydroxybutyrate inhibits class I histone deacetylases, inducing FOXO3A and metallothionein-2 and protecting mice against oxidative stress; fasting and CR raised histone acetylation in mouse tissues.

references.authors: de Cabo R, Mattson MP
references.title: Effects of Intermittent Fasting on Health, Aging, and Disease.
references.finding: Reviews metabolic switching and adaptive stress responses (including antioxidant defences) proposed to underlie fasting benefits.

references.authors: Sutton EF, Beyl R, Early KS, et al.
references.title: Early Time-Restricted Feeding Improves Insulin Sensitivity, Blood Pressure, and Oxidative Stress Even without Weight Loss in Men with Prediabetes.
references.finding: 5 weeks of 6-h early feeding (dinner before 3 pm) vs 12-h feeding, isocaloric and without weight loss, improved insulin sensitivity, blood pressure and plasma 8-isoprostane (~14%, P = 0.05).

references.authors: Cienfuegos S, Gabel K, Kalam F, et al.
references.title: Effects of 4- and 6-h Time-Restricted Feeding on Weight and Cardiometabolic Health: A Randomized Controlled Trial in Adults with Obesity.
references.finding: 8 weeks of 4-h or 6-h TRE cut intake ~550 kcal/day and weight ~3%, lowered 8-isoprostane by 34-37% vs control, did not change TNF-alpha or IL-6, and the 6-h group lost 1.5 kg lean mass.

references.authors: Peters B, Schwarz J, Schuppelius B, et al.
references.title: Intended isocaloric time-restricted eating shifts circadian clocks but does not improve cardiometabolic health in women with overweight.
references.finding: In an intended-isocaloric crossover, 2 weeks of early (8:00-16:00) or late (13:00-21:00) 8-h TRE did not improve insulin sensitivity, 24-h glucose, lipids, inflammatory or oxidative stress markers, though it shifted circadian phase.

references.authors: Wegman MP, Guo MH, Bennion DM, et al.
references.title: Practicality of intermittent fasting in humans and its effect on oxidative stress and genes related to aging and metabolism.
references.finding: Weight-stable alternate-day fasting (25%/175% days) for 3 weeks, with or without vitamins C and E, did not change oxidative stress markers; SIRT3 expression rose 2.7% and insulin fell slightly.

references.authors: Johnson JB, Summer W, Cutler RG, et al.
references.title: Alternate day calorie restriction improves clinical findings and reduces markers of oxidative stress and inflammation in overweight adults with moderate asthma.
references.finding: 8 weeks of alternate-day calorie restriction (8% weight loss) reduced 8-isoprostane, nitrotyrosine, protein carbonyls and HNE adducts (uncontrolled).

references.authors: Faris MA, Hussein RN, Al-Kurd RA, et al.
references.title: Impact of ramadan intermittent fasting on oxidative stress measured by urinary 15-f(2t)-isoprostane.
references.finding: Urinary 15-F2t-isoprostane rose by week 3 of Ramadan alongside gains in weight and body fat, suggesting the oxidative effect followed weight change, not fasting per se.

references.authors: Ibrahim WH, Habib HM, Jarrar AH, et al.
references.title: Effect of Ramadan fasting on markers of oxidative stress and serum biochemical markers of cellular damage in healthy subjects.
references.finding: Across Ramadan, erythrocyte MDA fell slightly while plasma protein carbonyls, glutathione, GPx, catalase and serum MDA were unchanged.

references.authors: Madkour MI, T El-Serafi A, Jahrami HA, et al.
references.title: Ramadan diurnal intermittent fasting modulates SOD2, TFAM, Nrf2, and sirtuins (SIRT1, SIRT3) gene expressions in subjects with overweight and obesity.
references.finding: After Ramadan, expression of TFAM, SOD2 and Nrf2 rose (by 90%, 54% and 412%) while SIRT3 fell 62%; gene expression only, no damage markers.

references.authors: Wilhelmi de Toledo F, Grundler F, Goutzourelas N, et al.
references.title: Influence of Long-Term Fasting on Blood Redox Status in Humans.
references.finding: A 10-day Buchinger fast lowered plasma TBARS and raised total antioxidant capacity alongside rising uric acid; erythrocyte GSH, GR, GPx and catalase were unchanged.

references.authors: Mojto V, Gvozdjakova A, Kucharska J, et al.
references.title: Effects of complete water fasting and regeneration diet on kidney function, oxidative stress and antioxidants.
references.finding: An 11-day water-only fast lowered TBARS, weight and blood pressure but raised uric acid and creatinine, lowered GFR and alpha-tocopherol; values normalised after refeeding.

references.authors: Il'yasova D, Fontana L, Bhapkar M, et al.
references.title: Effects of 2 years of caloric restriction on oxidative status assessed by urinary F2-isoprostanes: The CALERIE 2 randomized clinical trial.
references.finding: Prescribed 25% CR for 2 years (CALERIE 2) lowered urinary 2,3-dinor-iPF2alpha-III by 17%/13% and iPF2alpha-III by 20%/27% at 12/24 months vs ad libitum (LC-MS/MS).

references.authors: Redman LM, Smith SR, Burton JH, et al.
references.title: Metabolic Slowing and Reduced Oxidative Damage with Sustained Caloric Restriction Support the Rate of Living and Oxidative Damage Theories of Aging.
references.finding: ~15% CR sustained for 2 years (-8.7 kg) lowered 24-h energy expenditure 80-120 kcal/day beyond weight loss, reduced thyroid axis activity and lowered F2-isoprostane excretion.

references.authors: Heilbronn LK, de Jonge L, Frisard MI, et al.
references.title: Effect of 6-month calorie restriction on biomarkers of longevity, metabolic adaptation, and oxidative stress in overweight individuals: a randomized controlled trial.
references.finding: 6 months of 25% CR (or CR plus exercise) lowered fasting insulin and DNA damage; protein carbonyls were unchanged.

references.authors: Lowe DA, Wu N, Rohdin-Bibby L, et al.
references.title: Effects of Time-Restricted Eating on Weight Loss and Other Metabolic Parameters in Women and Men With Overweight and Obesity: The TREAT Randomized Clinical Trial.
references.finding: 12 weeks of 16:8 TRE (noon-8 pm) did not beat 3 structured meals (between-group -0.26 kg, NS) and reduced appendicular lean mass index more (-0.16 kg/m2).

references.authors: Liu D, Huang Y, Huang C, et al.
references.title: Calorie Restriction with or without Time-Restricted Eating in Weight Loss.
references.finding: With identical calorie targets for 12 months, 8-h TRE (8 am-4 pm) plus CR lost 8.0 kg vs 6.3 kg with CR alone (difference -1.8 kg, P = 0.11); no differences in fat, lean mass or metabolic risk factors.

references.authors: Jamshed H, Steger FL, Bryan DR, et al.
references.title: Effectiveness of Early Time-Restricted Eating for Weight Loss, Fat Loss, and Cardiometabolic Health in Adults With Obesity: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
references.finding: With matched weight-loss counselling, 8-h early TRE (7:00-15:00) lost 2.3 kg more than a >=12-h window over 14 weeks, equivalent to ~214 kcal/day extra restriction; body fat difference NS.

references.authors: Lin S, Cienfuegos S, Ezpeleta M, et al.
references.title: Time-Restricted Eating Without Calorie Counting for Weight Loss in a Racially Diverse Population : A Randomized Controlled Trial.
references.finding: Over 12 months, 8-h TRE (noon-8 pm) and 25% CR reduced intake similarly (~-425 vs -405 kcal/day) and weight similarly (-4.6 vs -5.4 kg vs control; difference NS).

references.authors: Xie Z, Sun Y, Ye Y, et al.
references.title: Randomized controlled trial for time-restricted eating in healthy volunteers without obesity.
references.finding: 5 weeks of early TRE improved insulin sensitivity, fasting glucose, adiposity and inflammation more than mid-day TRE.

references.authors: Manoogian ENC, Wilkinson MJ, O'Neal M, et al.
references.title: Time-Restricted Eating in Adults With Metabolic Syndrome : A Randomized Controlled Trial.
references.finding: Adding personalised 8-10-h TRE to standard care for 3 months lowered HbA1c by only 0.10% vs standard care alone.

references.authors: Jones R, Pabla P, Mallinson J, et al.
references.title: Two weeks of early time-restricted feeding (eTRF) improves skeletal muscle insulin and anabolic sensitivity in healthy men.
references.finding: 2 weeks of early TRF (08:00-16:00) improved whole-body insulin sensitivity and muscle glucose and BCAA uptake vs a control diet matched for the same ~400 kcal/day deficit and ~1 kg weight loss.

references.authors: Ravussin E, Beyl RA, Poggiogalle E, et al.
references.title: Early Time-Restricted Feeding Reduces Appetite and Increases Fat Oxidation But Does Not Affect Energy Expenditure in Humans.
references.finding: Isocaloric eating 8 am-2 pm vs 8 am-8 pm for 4 days did not change 24-h energy expenditure but lowered ghrelin and hunger and increased fat oxidation.

references.authors: Templeman I, Smith HA, Chowdhury E, et al.
references.title: A randomized controlled trial to isolate the effects of fasting and energy restriction on weight loss and metabolic health in lean adults.
references.finding: 3 weeks of 24-h alternate-day fasts with 150% intake on feed days lost similar weight to matched daily 25% CR but less fat (-0.74 vs -1.75 kg); fasting without energy deficit changed nothing; no fasting-specific metabolic benefit.

references.authors: Trepanowski JF, Kroeger CM, Barnosky A, et al.
references.title: Effect of Alternate-Day Fasting on Weight Loss, Weight Maintenance, and Cardioprotection Among Metabolically Healthy Obese Adults: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
references.finding: Over 1 year, alternate-day fasting (25%/125% days) and daily 25% CR produced the same weight loss (-6.0% vs -5.3% vs control) and cardiometabolic changes; ADF had more dropouts (38%).

references.authors: Stekovic S, Hofer SJ, Tripolt N, et al.
references.title: Alternate Day Fasting Improves Physiological and Molecular Markers of Aging in Healthy, Non-obese Humans.
references.finding: 4 weeks of strict 36-h/12-h alternate-day fasting cut intake 37%, reduced trunk fat, raised beta-hydroxybutyrate even on eating days, and lowered sICAM-1, LDL and T3 after long-term ADF, without adverse events.

references.authors: Harvie MN, Pegington M, Mattson MP, et al.
references.title: The effects of intermittent or continuous energy restriction on weight loss and metabolic disease risk markers: a randomized trial in young overweight women.
references.finding: Over 6 months, 2 days/week of ~650 kcal (5:2-type) and continuous 25% restriction lost similar weight (-6.4 vs -5.6 kg) with slightly greater falls in fasting insulin and HOMA-IR with intermittent restriction.

references.authors: Sundfør TM, Svendsen M, Tonstad S
references.title: Effect of intermittent versus continuous energy restriction on weight loss, maintenance and cardiometabolic risk: A randomized 1-year trial.
references.finding: Over 1 year, 400/600 kcal on 2 non-consecutive days/week matched continuous restriction for weight loss (-8.0 vs -9.0 kg) and maintenance, with more hunger.

references.authors: Carter S, Clifton PM, Keogh JB
references.title: Effect of Intermittent Compared With Continuous Energy Restricted Diet on Glycemic Control in Patients With Type 2 Diabetes: A Randomized Noninferiority Trial.
references.finding: Over 12 months, 2 days/week of 500-600 kcal was equivalent to continuous 1200-1500 kcal/day for HbA1c (-0.3% vs -0.5%), with medication reduction to manage hypoglycaemia.

references.authors: Wei M, Brandhorst S, Shelehchi M, et al.
references.title: Fasting-mimicking diet and markers/risk factors for aging, diabetes, cancer, and cardiovascular disease.
references.finding: Three monthly 5-day fasting-mimicking diet cycles lowered body weight, trunk fat, blood pressure and IGF-1 vs usual diet, with larger changes in people at higher baseline risk.

references.authors: Brandhorst S, Choi IY, Wei M, et al.
references.title: A Periodic Diet that Mimics Fasting Promotes Multi-System Regeneration, Enhanced Cognitive Performance, and Healthspan.
references.finding: Bimonthly 4-day FMD cycles in mice extended lifespan, cut visceral fat and cancer incidence and lowered IGF-1; a pilot trial of 3 cycles reduced human risk markers.

references.authors: Brandhorst S, Levine ME, Wei M, et al.
references.title: Fasting-mimicking diet causes hepatic and blood markers changes indicating reduced biological age and disease risk.
references.finding: Exploratory analysis: 3 FMD cycles were associated with lower insulin resistance and liver fat and a 2.5-year drop in a blood-chemistry biological age estimate.

references.authors: Wilhelmi de Toledo F, Grundler F, Bergouignan A, et al.
references.title: Safety, health improvement and well-being during a 4 to 21-day fasting period in an observational study including 1422 subjects.
references.finding: Buchinger fasts of 4-21 days at 200-250 kcal/day lowered weight, waist and blood pressure, raised ketones and were well tolerated, with adverse effects in <1% (uncontrolled, clinic-affiliated authors).

references.authors: Finnell JS, Saul BC, Goldhamer AC, et al.
references.title: Is fasting safe? A chart review of adverse events during medically supervised, water-only fasting.
references.finding: Among supervised water-only fasts of >=2 days, most adverse events were mild (fatigue, insomnia, nausea, headache), 212 visits had a grade 3 event, and one grade 4 hyponatraemia occurred on day 9 in a 70-year-old.

references.authors: Laurens C, Grundler F, Damiot A, et al.
references.title: Is muscle and protein loss relevant in long-term fasting in healthy men? A prospective trial on physiological adaptations.
references.finding: A 10-day fast (200-250 kcal/day) cut weight 5.9 kg, ~60% lean soft tissue (mostly water and glycogen; 42% metabolically active tissue), lowered BMR 12%, and preserved strength; urinary BHB plateaued from day 4.

references.authors: Fernando HA, Zibellini J, Harris RA, et al.
references.title: Effect of Ramadan Fasting on Weight and Body Composition in Healthy Non-Athlete Adults: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
references.finding: Ramadan fasting produced small, transient weight and fat losses (fat % fell only in people with overweight), with some fat-free mass loss, largely regained 2-5 weeks later.

references.authors: Allaf M, Elghazaly H, Mohamed OG, et al.
references.title: Intermittent fasting for the prevention of cardiovascular disease.
references.finding: Cochrane: IF beat ad libitum eating for short-term weight (-2.88 kg) but showed no clinically meaningful difference from continuous energy restriction (-0.88 kg short term, -0.56 kg medium term); no hard CVD outcome data.

references.authors: Patikorn C, Roubal K, Veettil SK, et al.
references.title: Intermittent Fasting and Obesity-Related Health Outcomes: An Umbrella Review of Meta-analyses of Randomized Clinical Trials.
references.finding: Umbrella review: most IF benefits were supported by low or very-low quality evidence; only modified ADF for BMI reached high quality, and IF was associated with reduced fat-free mass.

references.authors: Semnani-Azad Z, Khan TA, Chiavaroli L, et al.
references.title: Intermittent fasting strategies and their effects on body weight and other cardiometabolic risk factors: systematic review and network meta-analysis of randomised clinical trials.
references.finding: Network meta-analysis: all IF forms and continuous restriction beat ad libitum eating; vs continuous restriction only ADF showed a small extra weight loss (-1.29 kg, moderate certainty).

references.authors: Kraus WE, Bhapkar M, Huffman KM, et al.
references.title: 2 years of calorie restriction and cardiometabolic risk (CALERIE): exploratory outcomes of a multicentre, phase 2, randomised controlled trial.
references.finding: CALERIE: achieved 11.9% CR for 2 years (-7.5 kg, 71% fat) lowered LDL, total/HDL ratio, blood pressure, CRP and insulin resistance vs control.

references.authors: Waziry R, Ryan CP, Corcoran DL, et al.
references.title: Effect of long-term caloric restriction on DNA methylation measures of biological aging in healthy adults from the CALERIE trial.
references.finding: Post hoc CALERIE analysis: 2 years of CR slowed the DunedinPACE pace-of-aging methylation measure (small effect) but did not change PhenoAge or GrimAge clocks.

references.authors: Fontana L, Weiss EP, Villareal DT, et al.
references.title: Long-term effects of calorie or protein restriction on serum IGF-1 and IGFBP-3 concentration in humans.
references.finding: Long-term severe CR without malnutrition did not lower serum IGF-1 in humans, whereas reducing protein from 1.67 to 0.95 g/kg/day for 3 weeks lowered IGF-1 from 194 to 152 ng/mL.

references.authors: Villareal DT, Fontana L, Das SK, et al.
references.title: Effect of Two-Year Caloric Restriction on Bone Metabolism and Bone Mineral Density in Non-Obese Younger Adults: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
references.finding: 2 years of CR (-7.5 kg, including -2.2 kg fat-free mass) reduced lumbar spine, hip and femoral neck BMD vs ad libitum and raised bone resorption markers.

references.authors: Chen M, Xu L, Van Horn L, et al.
references.title: Association of eating duration less than 8 h with all-cause, cardiovascular, and cancer mortality.
references.finding: Eating duration <8 h on two 24-h recalls (~2% of participants, more often smokers, food-insecure and breakfast-skippers) was associated with higher cardiovascular mortality (HR 2.35, 1.39-3.98) vs 12-14 h but not robustly with all-cause or cancer mortality; requiring <8 h on both days gave HR 1.78 (NS).

references.authors: Mehanna HM, Moledina J, Travis J
references.title: Refeeding syndrome: what it is, and how to prevent and treat it.
references.finding: NICE-based refeeding risk criteria include little or no intake for >10 days (one criterion alone) or >5 days (with another factor), plus low potassium, phosphate or magnesium before feeding.

references.authors: Friedli N, Stanga Z, Sobotka L, et al.
references.title: Revisiting the refeeding syndrome: Results of a systematic review.
references.finding: Systematic review: refeeding syndrome definitions vary widely (incidence 0-80%), but it occurs mostly within 72 h of restarting nutrition.

references.authors: Sichieri R, Everhart JE, Roth H
references.title: A prospective study of hospitalization with gallstone disease among women: role of dietary factors, fasting period, and dieting.
references.finding: Over 10 years, risk of hospitalisation with gallstone disease rose with longer overnight fasting periods and with dieting; fibre was mildly protective.

references.authors: Yang H, Petersen GM, Roth MP, et al.
references.title: Risk factors for gallstone formation during rapid loss of weight.
references.finding: 10.9% developed gallstones within 16 weeks of rapid weight loss on a very-low-calorie diet; higher BMI and greater BMI loss raised risk.

references.authors: Corley BT, Carroll RW, Hall RM, et al.
references.title: Intermittent fasting in Type 2 diabetes mellitus and the risk of hypoglycaemia: a randomized controlled trial.
references.finding: Two 500-600 kcal days/week roughly doubled hypoglycaemia rate in people on glucose-lowering drugs despite medication reduction (RR 2.05), whether fast days were consecutive or not.

references.authors: Hassanein M, Al-Arouj M, Hamdy O, et al.
references.title: Diabetes and Ramadan: Practical guidelines.
references.finding: IDF-DAR practical guidelines for fasting with diabetes: risk stratification, nutrition advice and medication adjustment for insulin and sulfonylureas.

references.authors: Ganson KT, Cuccolo K, Hallward L, et al.
references.title: Intermittent fasting: Describing engagement and associations with eating disorder behaviors and psychopathology among Canadian adolescents and young adults.
references.finding: Almost half of Canadian young people reported intermittent fasting in the past year, and it was associated with eating-disorder behaviours and psychopathology, most consistently in women.

references.authors: Mountjoy M, Ackerman KE, Bailey DM, et al.
references.title: 2023 International Olympic Committee's (IOC) consensus statement on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport (REDs).
references.finding: IOC consensus on Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport: low energy availability impairs reproductive, bone, metabolic and other systems in all sexes.

references.authors: Cameron JL, Weltzin TE, McConaha C, et al.
references.title: Slowing of pulsatile luteinizing hormone secretion in men after forty-eight hours of fasting.
references.finding: 48 h of fasting cut mean LH from 2.94 to 1.07 IU/L and halved LH pulse frequency, and lowered FSH and testosterone, without a rise in cortisol.

references.authors: Moro T, Tinsley G, Bianco A, et al.
references.title: Effects of eight weeks of time-restricted feeding (16/8) on basal metabolism, maximal strength, body composition, inflammation, and cardiovascular risk factors in resistance-trained males.
references.finding: 8 weeks of isocaloric 16:8 TRE with resistance training reduced fat mass, preserved lean mass and strength, but lowered testosterone, IGF-1 and T3.

references.authors: Cienfuegos S, Corapi S, Gabel K, et al.
references.title: Effect of Intermittent Fasting on Reproductive Hormone Levels in Females and Males: A Review of Human Trials.
references.finding: Review of human trials: IF lowers testosterone/free androgen index and raises SHBG in premenopausal women with obesity, does not change oestrogen or gonadotropins, and lowers testosterone in lean active young men.

references.authors: Poursalehian M, Mohseni S, Shadman Z, et al.
references.title: Impact of Ramadan fasting on serum levels of major endocrinology hormonal and biochemical parameters in healthy non-athlete adults: A systematic review and meta-analyses.
references.finding: Ramadan fasting did not significantly change testosterone, LH, FSH, prolactin or thyroid hormones in healthy non-athletes; morning cortisol tended to fall.

references.authors: Engel OJ, Doctory N, Sun B, et al.
references.title: The Effect of Month-Long Daily Fasting on Semen Parameters: A Retrospective Cohort Study.
references.finding: Semen samples produced during Ramadan (and 70 days after) had lower post-gradient progressive motility (30% vs 38%) and lower volume than the same men's samples at other times (retrospective).

references.authors: Abbas SM, Basalamah AH
references.title: Effects of Ramadhan fast on male fertility.
references.finding: Small study: Ramadan did not harm semen in healthy men; LH and semen volume fell after the fast while sperm count rose during it.

references.authors: May KT, Behling J, Sochiera-Plegniere K, et al.
references.title: Fasting for male fertility-a mixed methods study.
references.finding: Three 5-day 500 kcal FMD cycles over 4 months produced no clear differences in semen parameters vs waiting-list controls (pilot, underpowered).

references.authors: Loucks AB, Thuma JR
references.title: Luteinizing hormone pulsatility is disrupted at a threshold of energy availability in regularly menstruating women.
references.finding: LH pulsatility was unaffected at an energy availability of 30 kcal/kg lean mass/day but disrupted below that threshold (10-20 kcal/kg).

references.authors: Olson BR, Cartledge T, Sebring N, et al.
references.title: Short-term fasting affects luteinizing hormone secretory dynamics but not reproductive function in normal-weight sedentary women.
references.finding: A 3-day mid-follicular fast reduced LH pulses but did not alter follicle growth, ovulation or cycle length in normal-weight women.

references.authors: Alvero R, Kimzey L, Sebring N, et al.
references.title: Effects of fasting on neuroendocrine function and follicle development in lean women.
references.finding: In lean women a 72-h follicular-phase fast cut LH pulses 19%; 2 of 7 fasted cycles were anovulatory and follicular phases lengthened.

references.authors: Li C, Xing C, Zhang J, et al.
references.title: Eight-hour time-restricted feeding improves endocrine and metabolic profiles in women with anovulatory polycystic ovary syndrome.
references.finding: 5 weeks of 8-h TRE (single arm) lowered weight, testosterone, free androgen index, insulin and hsCRP, raised SHBG, and improved menstrual regularity in 11 of 15 women.

references.authors: Talebi S, Shab-Bidar S, Moini A, et al.
references.title: The effects of time-restricted eating alone or in combination with probiotic supplementation in comparison with a calorie-restricted diet on endocrine and metabolic profiles in women with polycystic ovary syndrome: A randomized clinical trial.
references.finding: 8 weeks of 14:10 early TRE (with or without probiotics) gave no greater weight loss or menstrual, androgen or metabolic improvement than daily calorie restriction.

references.authors: Ranneh Y, Hamsho M, Shkorfu W, et al.
references.title: Effect of Intermittent Fasting on Anthropometric Measurements, Metabolic Profile, and Hormones in Women with Polycystic Ovary Syndrome: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
references.finding: In PCOS, IF reduced weight (-4.25 kg), insulin resistance, free androgen index and DHEA-S and raised SHBG; total testosterone and AMH did not change.

references.authors: Glazier JD, Hayes DJL, Hussain S, et al.
references.title: The effect of Ramadan fasting during pregnancy on perinatal outcomes: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Ramadan fasting in pregnancy did not affect birth weight or preterm delivery; lower placental weight came mainly from one large study; no perinatal mortality data.

references.authors: Al-Taiar A, Rahman ME, Salama M, et al.
references.title: Impacts of Ramadan fasting during pregnancy on pregnancy and birth outcomes: An umbrella review.
references.finding: Umbrella review: insufficient evidence that Ramadan fasting in pregnancy shortens gestation or reduces birth weight, but evidence quality is low and no firm guidance is possible.

references.authors: Metzger BE, Ravnikar V, Vileisis RA, et al.
references.title: "Accelerated starvation" and the skipped breakfast in late normal pregnancy.
references.finding: Extending the overnight fast from 12 to 18 h in late pregnancy ('skipped breakfast') caused falling glucose and rising fatty acids and beta-hydroxybutyrate ('accelerated starvation'); non-pregnant women barely changed.

references.authors: Rizzo T, Metzger BE, Burns WJ, et al.
references.title: Correlations between antepartum maternal metabolism and intelligence of offspring.
references.finding: Higher third-trimester maternal beta-hydroxybutyrate correlated with lower offspring IQ scores at ages 2-5 (r about -0.2), observational.

references.authors: Aird TP, Davies RW, Carson BP
references.title: Effects of fasted vs fed-state exercise on performance and post-exercise metabolism: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Pre-exercise feeding improved prolonged aerobic performance but not shorter exercise; fasted exercise raised post-exercise fatty acids and muscle signalling linked to mitochondrial adaptation.

references.authors: Edinburgh RM, Bradley HE, Abdullah NF, et al.
references.title: Lipid Metabolism Links Nutrient-Exercise Timing to Insulin Sensitivity in Men Classified as Overweight or Obese.
references.finding: 6 weeks of cycling performed before vs after carbohydrate intake lowered postprandial insulin and improved oral glucose insulin sensitivity, linked to greater lipid use during exercise.

references.authors: Tinsley GM, Moore ML, Graybeal AJ, et al.
references.title: Time-restricted feeding plus resistance training in active females: a randomized trial.
references.finding: 8 weeks of ~7.5-h TRE with resistance training and adequate protein (1.6 g/kg) produced the same lean-mass and strength gains as a normal schedule.

references.authors: Faris MAE, Jahrami HA, Alhayki FA, et al.
references.title: Effect of diurnal fasting on sleep during Ramadan: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: During Ramadan total sleep time fell from ~7.2 to ~6.4 h/night with a negligible change in daytime sleepiness.

references.authors: Clavero-Jimeno A, Dote-Montero M, Migueles JH, et al.
references.title: Time-Restricted Eating and Sleep, Mood, and Quality of Life in Adults With Overweight or Obesity: A Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Clinical Trial.
references.finding: 12 weeks of early, late or self-selected 8-h TRE did not change sleep, mood or quality of life vs usual care.
